definition: The shining, immortal spirit the deceased becomes after a favourable judgement, when their ka and ba are reunited.
“What is in the Duat”: a New Kingdom funerary book, carved in the royal tombs, which describes hour by hour the night journey of the sun through the underworld.
A hieroglyph shaped like a cross topped by a loop, meaning “life”. The gods hold it in their hand and offer it to the king.
The white crown of Upper Egypt flanked by two ostrich feathers, worn above all by Osiris.
Often translated as “soul”: the personality of the deceased, shown as a bird with a human head, free to leave the tomb by day and return to it at night.
The mound of earth that first rose from the waters of the Nun, on which the creator stood. The tips of pyramids and obelisks are its image.
The sacred bird of Heliopolis, similar to a heron, in whose form the creator appeared on the Benben. The Greeks likened it to the phoenix.
The four jars holding the organs removed from the deceased during embalming: the liver, lungs, stomach and intestines, each protected by a son of Horus and a goddess.
Middle Kingdom funerary spells, painted inside coffins, which extended to private individuals the spells once reserved for the king.
The god who created the world (from the Greek dēmiourgos, “craftsman”). Each great Egyptian cosmogony has its own: Atum, Ptah, Amun or the Ogdoad.
A pillar symbolising stability, often interpreted as the backbone of Osiris.
The body, which embalming was meant to preserve so that the ka and ba could return to it.
The pschent, which combines the white crown of Upper Egypt and the red crown of Lower Egypt, symbol of the king of the Two Lands.
The underworld of the dead, which the sun crosses every night and through which the deceased travels to the tribunal of Osiris.
The group of nine gods of Heliopolis: Atum, Shu, Tefnut, Geb, Nut, Osiris, Isis, Seth and Nephthys. The word also refers to the assembly of the gods.
The five days added at the end of the 360-day year, during which the children of Nut were born.
The paradise of the justified dead, an ideal Egypt with plentiful harvests.
The sacred writing of the Egyptians, made of pictorial signs, whose invention was credited to Thoth. It was deciphered by Champollion in 1822.
Disorder, injustice and falsehood, the opposites of Maat, which the king and the gods must constantly drive back.
The life force, born with the individual and outliving them. It fed on the offerings left in the tomb.
A collection of spells, written on papyrus and placed in the tomb, which helped the deceased overcome the dangers of the afterlife. The Egyptians called it the “Book of Coming Forth by Day”.
A natural salt gathered from dried-up lakes, used to dry out the body during embalming.
A list of wrongs the deceased declared they had not committed, before the forty-two judges of the tribunal of Osiris.
A province of ancient Egypt. The country had about forty of them, each with its own capital and gods.
The primordial ocean, inert and dark, which existed before Creation and still surrounds the ordered world.
A tall standing stone with a pyramid-shaped tip, a solar symbol, set up in front of temples.
The group of eight gods of Hermopolis, four couples embodying the chaos before Creation: Nun and Naunet, Heh and Hauhet, Kek and Kauket, Amun and Amaunet.
A rite performed on the mummy before burial, which gave the deceased back the use of their senses.
The weighing of the heart of the deceased against the feather of Maat, at the judgement of the dead.
The oldest Egyptian religious texts, carved inside the royal pyramids from the end of the 5th Dynasty onwards.
The name, an essential part of the self: as long as it was spoken, the deceased went on existing.
The underground galleries at Saqqara where the mummified Apis bulls were buried.
The shadow, an element inseparable from the person.
A sacred musical instrument made of metal rods that jingle when shaken, associated with Hathor and Bastet.
An upright stone slab bearing an inscription or an image.
A divine family made up of a god, a goddess and their child, such as Amun, Mut and Khonsu at Thebes.
Upper Egypt (the valley, in the south) and Lower Egypt (the Delta, in the north), united under the authority of a single king.
The Eye of Horus, healed after his struggle against Seth, an amulet of protection and a symbol of wholeness.
The rearing cobra worn on the brow of kings and gods, image of the goddess Wadjet, ready to spit fire at their enemies.
A sceptre with an animal head and a forked base, symbol of power, held by the gods.
